title: Capturing lost signals and sunlight to power satellites
sourceTitle: Capturing lost signals and sunlight to power satellites
headline: Capturing Lost Sunlight for Satellites
author: Jonathan O’Callaghan
attribution: This article was originally published in Horizon, the EU Research and Innovation magazine. Original reporting by Jonathan O’Callaghan; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Satellites need electricity. They use solar panels, but some sunlight is not used. Some radio waves also travel past their targets.
A European research team wants to collect a little of this lost energy. The team is testing very small antennas.
One kind could turn stray radio waves into electricity. Another kind could collect infrared light from the Sun.
The researchers hope these devices will give satellites extra power. They are still testing the idea.

evidence: Satellites waste energy in space. Some radio waves spill beyond their intended targets, while some of the sunlight reaching a spacecraft falls outside the range that conventional solar panels can effectively capture. Researchers from seven European countries are working together to see if some of that lost energy can be recovered.

The initiative, called POWERSAT and supported by the European Innovation Council, is developing tiny devices that could harvest stray radio waves and infrared sunlight, giving satellites an extra source of energy.

In space, every watt of power and every gram of mass matters. Satellites have limited room for power systems, while adding equipment can increase the weight and cost of a mission. Could recovering energy that would otherwise be lost provide a useful boost?
A1-A2.headline: Satellites May Use More Sunlight

pages.text: A project called POWERSAT is exploring ways to recover energy that satellites currently lose.

Radio signals can spread beyond their intended destination, while ordinary solar panels do not capture all of the Sun’s infrared light. Researchers from several European countries are studying both sources.
The team is developing compact antennas that could convert spilled radio energy into electricity. It is also working on tiny structures for infrared light.
Spacecraft have strict limits on weight and room, so any extra power must come from devices small enough to fit. The approach remains under development.

pages.text: POWERSAT addresses a practical constraint in satellite engineering: a spacecraft has limited mass and surface area, yet its instruments depend on reliable electrical power.
The project examines energy already present around a satellite, including radio-frequency spillover and infrared sunlight that conventional panels use poorly.

Researchers envisage miniature rectennas near communications equipment and tiny antennas alongside existing solar panels. Those devices would supplement established power systems rather than replace them.
Their promise depends on whether they can survive orbital conditions and deliver a useful gain without adding prohibitive weight or complexity.

title: New advanced materials could give electric motors an efficiency boost
sourceTitle: New advanced materials could give electric motors an efficiency boost
headline: Advanced Materials Could Boost Electric Motors
author: Anthony King
attribution: This article was originally published in Horizon, the EU Research and Innovation magazine. Original reporting by Anthony King; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Electric motors work in many machines, from washing machines to factory tools. They use a lot of electricity across Europe.
Even a small improvement in each motor could save energy when many motors are in use.
Researchers in Europe are testing a new kind of metal for motor parts. Its structure may help the motor lose less energy as heat.
They have also made test parts with metal 3D printing. The work is promising, but the new parts still need more testing.

evidence: Electric motors are the largely unseen workhorses of modern life. They power everything from washing machines to factory equipment. Individually, many are already highly efficient. But because there are billions of them, even small improvements could translate into significant energy savings.

When Spanish scientist Dr María Teresa Pérez Prado found out just how much of Europe’s electricity is consumed by electric motors, she was astonished: they were estimated to account for more than 50% of all electricity consumed in the EU in 2020.
“When I discovered these numbers, I was completely amazed,” she said – and it became a lasting source of motivation in her work.
A1-A2.headline: New Materials Help Electric Motors Work Better

pages.text: Europe uses electric motors throughout homes and industry. Many individual motors are already efficient, but the huge number in service makes small gains valuable.
Researchers involved in the AM2SoftMag project have studied advanced magnetic materials that may reduce energy lost inside motors.

One candidate is metallic glass, whose atoms do not form the regular pattern found in ordinary metals. Researchers have used carefully controlled metal 3D printing to produce components while preserving that structure.
The results show a manufacturing route, but they do not mean every existing motor can already be replaced.

B1-B2.headline: Advanced Materials Could Boost Electric Motors

pages.text: The scale of motor use makes incremental efficiency gains economically significant. European researchers are examining whether advanced soft magnetic materials can cut losses caused by changing magnetic fields inside an electric motor.

Their work links materials science to wider efforts to reduce electricity demand during electrification. The AM2SoftMag team reports producing motor components from metallic glass with laser-based additive manufacturing.
Cooling conditions matter because excessive heat can destroy the disordered structure responsible for the material’s properties.
This is a research advance in component production; commercial performance and deployment still require further validation.

title: The hidden link between Europe’s housing crisis and energy poverty
sourceTitle: The hidden link between Europe’s housing crisis and energy poverty
headline: Europe’s Housing Crisis and Energy Poverty
author: Gareth Willmer
attribution: This article was originally published in Horizon, the EU Research and Innovation magazine. Original reporting by Gareth Willmer; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: A home can cost too much even when the rent looks possible to pay. People must also pay for heating and sometimes cooling.
Some older homes use a lot of energy, so families can face two problems at once. A European research project is studying housing costs and energy costs together.
Its team looks at local projects for people with low incomes and other groups who need help.
The researchers hope cities can learn from these projects and make homes both affordable and comfortable.

evidence: As cities across Europe sweltered under a heatwave in June 2026, professor Michael Janoschka was focused on a longer term problem: how to make homes affordable and energy-efficient in a continent facing a housing crisis.
Janoschka has spent much of his career studying how rising house prices, property speculation and urban inequality are reshaping European cities.

Today, as professor of regional science at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology in Germany, he is leading an international team investigating how housing affordability and energy poverty can be tackled together rather than as separate policy challenges.
A1-A2.headline: Europe’s Homes Can Cost More to Heat

pages.text: Researchers working on Europe’s housing crisis argue that rent, mortgages and energy bills should be considered together.
Older, inefficient homes can be expensive to heat or cool, adding pressure to households that are already struggling with housing costs.

The EU-supported PREFIGURE project is studying local approaches across several European countries. Its team has examined programmes that combine affordable housing with energy improvements, including work with municipalities and housing organisations.
The researchers are assessing which lessons might transfer between cities rather than assuming that one scheme will work everywhere.

pages.text: Housing affordability is often measured through purchase prices or rent, but that view can obscure the continuing cost of keeping a home at a safe temperature.
The PREFIGURE researchers treat housing and energy poverty as linked policy problems, especially where older buildings are inefficient and vulnerable households face multiple pressures.
Their international study compares local initiatives and surveys households to identify approaches that may be adapted elsewhere.

Examples in Karlsruhe, Thessaloniki and Barcelona involve combinations of renovation, social housing and community participation. The report presents these as developing policy lessons, not as proof of a single universal solution.

title: Casting a wider net: digital tools bring Europe’s fisheries into sharper focus
sourceTitle: Casting a wider net: digital tools bring Europe’s fisheries into sharper focus
headline: Digital Tools for Europe’s Fisheries
author: Michael Allen
attribution: This article was originally published in Horizon, the EU Research and Innovation magazine. Original reporting by Michael Allen; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: People who catch fish and people who protect fish stocks both need good information. But scientists cannot watch every fishing boat.
They may not know exactly which fish are caught at sea. A European project is testing cameras and computer tools on boats.
The tools may help count and identify fish. Better records could help fishers, scientists and officials make decisions.
The project is still testing how well its systems work in real fishing conditions.

evidence: Europe’s fishing fleets land 3.2 million tonnes of fish a year, worth €5.5 billion. Yet fishers, scientists and regulators still lack a complete picture of what is happening at sea.

In Belgium, for example, which has only around 60 fishing vessels, onboard scientific sampling currently covers just 1.5% of fishing trips, said Els Torreele. She leads fisheries research at the Flanders Research Institute for Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (ILVO) in Belgium.
“We don’t have enough data to cover all we need to know about what is going on in the sea or with the stock,” she said.
A1-A2.headline: Digital Tools Help Europe’s Fishers

pages.text: European fisheries need reliable catch data, but traditional observation covers only part of the activity at sea.
Incomplete records can make it harder for scientists to assess fish stocks and for fishers to understand decisions about catch limits.

The EU-funded OptiFish project is developing digital monitoring tools, including cameras and AI systems that recognise species. Researchers from several countries are testing the technology on different types of fishing operations.
They hope more complete data will support fairer management, while acknowledging that the quality of the measurements must be checked.

B1-B2.headline: Digital Tools for Europe’s Fisheries

pages.text: Fisheries policy depends on credible estimates of what is caught, where it is caught and which species are involved.
The Horizon report describes a persistent evidence gap: manual observers and sampling cannot cover every trip, and incomplete information can strain trust between fishing communities and regulators.

OptiFish is combining computer vision, electronic monitoring and other techniques to improve the record. Its researchers are testing identification systems across varied vessels and checking for errors when fish overlap or are partly hidden.
Better monitoring could inform stock assessments and quotas, but the project is still developing and validating its methods.
